q: What limitations of the Transformer do the authors themselves acknowledge?
text:
The paper has no dedicated limitations section, so the acknowledgements are scattered through the text and the future-work plans.

The first is reduced resolution. Relating any two positions in a constant number of operations comes "at the cost of reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions," which multi-head attention is meant to counteract p. 2.

The second is long sequences. Self-attention is cheaper per layer than recurrence only when the sequence length n is smaller than the representation dimension d p. 6. For very long sequences the authors propose restricting attention to a neighbourhood of size r, which would lengthen the maximum path to O(n/r), and they leave this for future work p. 7. The document never says "quadratic," so reading the cost as quadratic in n is my inference from the complexity table.

The third is the attention scoring function. Reducing the key size dk hurts quality, which the authors take to suggest that "a more sophisticated compatibility function than dot product may be beneficial" p. 9. Quality also drops with too many heads p. 9.

The fourth is sequential generation. The decoder is auto-regressive, producing one element at a time p. 2. The conclusion lists "making generation less sequential" as a goal p. 10.

The fifth is scope. Extending the model to images, audio and video, and to input and output modalities other than text, is stated as a plan rather than something shown p. 10. On parsing, the model beats all earlier results except the Recurrent Neural Network Grammar, and only a small number of experiments were run to choose dropout, learning rates and beam size p. 10.

q: How does the base model differ from the big model, and what did each cost to train?
text:
The two differ in size, dropout and training length. The details are on pages 7, 8 and 9.

Base model: 6 layers, dmodel 512, dff 2048, 8 heads with dk = dv = 64, dropout 0.1, 100K steps, about 65 million parameters p. 9. Big model: 6 layers, dmodel 1024, dff 4096, 16 heads, dropout 0.3, 300K steps, about 213 million parameters p. 9. Table 3 does not list dk and dv for the big model. The English-to-French big model used dropout 0.1 instead of 0.3 p. 8.

Training cost, all on one machine with 8 P100 GPUs: the base model took about 0.4 seconds per step, so 100,000 steps took roughly 12 hours. The big model took 1.0 second per step, so 300,000 steps took 3.5 days p. 7.

The FLOP estimates in Table 2 are 3.3 for base and 2.3 for big, but the exponents were lost in the text I have, so I can't give the actual figures. The authors estimated them as training time times number of GPUs times sustained per-GPU capacity, using 9.5 TFLOPS for the P100 p. 8.

In quality, the base model scores 27.3 (English-German) and 38.1 (English-French) BLEU, and the big model 28.4 and 41.8 p. 8. The text on page 8 gives 41.0 for the big model on English-French, which conflicts with the 41.8 in the abstract and table.
